clue.text: One offering unwanted advice to support troubled advertiser

indicators.note: something troubled is disturbed and thrown into disorder, so these letters are jumbled

blocks.note: to back someone is to support them
the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone helps a struggling advertising man while lecturing him with advice nobody asked for.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition comes first and the support after it, yet the support supplies the opening letters; the leftover word happens to hold the exact ten letters of the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a passenger who tells the driver how to drive, and by extension anyone giving unwelcome instructions.

clue.text: A night at the pub may give you it when you want it

definitions.text: A night at the pub may give you it when you want it

blocks.clueFragment: A night at the pub may give you it
blocks.note: surface reading: a hangover, or some other unwelcome souvenir of heavy drinking
setter's reading: 'it' is sex, and what drink causes is failure to perform at exactly the moment desired

explanation.surface: A night of drinking leaves you with something just when you are hoping for something else.
explanation.walkthrough: The two uses of 'it' do different jobs: the first is the affliction, the second is sex. The phrase is British slang named after the brewer of beer.
explanation.definitionFit: This British slang term names temporary male impotence caused by drinking too much alcohol, typically beer.

clue.text: Drinks cold water on leaving bar upset

indicators.note: the little word is taken out as if it walked away from the rest
in a down answer, upset means turned upside down, so the letters read bottom to top

blocks.note: C marks the cold-water tap
a saloon is a bar; ON is removed from SALOON

explanation.surface: Someone in a pub pours cold water on their drinks after an upset.
explanation.walkthrough: SALOON loses ON to give SALO; with C it makes SALOC, which reads upwards as the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Cola is a sweet fizzy soft drink, and the plural gives several servings of it.

clue.text: Release volume dismissing an old rugby player

indicators.note: to dismiss is to send away, so a letter is sent out of the word

blocks.note: to spring a prisoner is to release them
a volume is a book
O is the abbreviation for old; one of them goes

explanation.surface: An old rugby player retires and publishes his memoirs, then drops them.
explanation.walkthrough: BOOK has two O's; 'an old' removes just one of them.
explanation.definitionFit: The Springboks are South Africa's national rugby union team, so any member is called by that name.

clue.text: After a month, satisfied to receive new increase

indicators.note: to receive something is to take it in, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: the calendar abbreviation for August
a need that is met is satisfied
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: After a month of waiting, someone is pleased to get a pay rise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' here is a placing instruction: the month leads, and everything else follows it.
explanation.definitionFit: To augment something is to make it larger or add to it, a direct verb synonym.

clue.text: Stop papers reversing demand about book

indicators.note: reversing means going backwards, so the word is read in the opposite direction
about means around, so one word wraps round another

blocks.note: identity papers are your ID
a sale is demand for goods, as in 'there is no sale for it'
B is the abbreviation for book

explanation.surface: Newspapers changing their position on a demand made about a book.
explanation.walkthrough: Sale meaning demand is a genuine dictionary sense, as when a product 'finds no sale'.
explanation.definitionFit: To disable a machine or device is to stop it working, so the verb fits as a synonym.

clue.text: Still no start of better time

indicators.note: with no start, a word has lost its opening letter

blocks.note: finer means better; its first letter goes
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Things are still no better, and no sign of improvement yet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' reads as the adverb 'yet', but it is the adjective meaning motionless. FINER is the better that loses its head.
explanation.definitionFit: Something inert lies motionless and lacks the power to move, so it is still.

clue.text: Scientist’s wife abandoning marriage fashion

indicators.note: abandoning means leaving behind, so a letter walks out of the word

blocks.note: W is the abbreviation for wife, and it is the letter dropped
a wedding is a marriage; W goes from the front
ton is an old word for the fashionable style or set

explanation.surface: A scientist's wife walks out of the marriage, perhaps over fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scientist’s' looks possessive but the ’s is 'is'. TON for fashion comes from French bon ton.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Arthur Eddington was the English astrophysicist who confirmed Einstein's prediction about light bending during an eclipse.

clue.text: Mathematician’s principle, first to last attached to basis of logarithms

indicators.note: the opening letter is moved round to become the final one

blocks.note: e is the base of natural logarithms
a rule is a principle; R moves to the end

explanation.surface: Describes a mathematician's principle in logarithms, fitting since he gave his name to the constant e.
explanation.walkthrough: The number e is sometimes called Euler's number, so the surface is apt. 'Basis' stands for the mathematical base.
explanation.definitionFit: Leonhard Euler was the prolific eighteenth-century Swiss mathematician behind much of modern notation.

clue.text: Date energy stabilised

blocks.note: go means energy or vigour
something stabilised is steady

explanation.surface: A calendar date on which a supply of energy was finally stabilised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Date' looks like a noun for a day; it is the verb for courting.
explanation.definitionFit: To go steady is an old idiom for being in a regular romantic relationship with one partner.

clue.text: Unexpectedly chose to inhale pot – resounding effects in these places

indicators.note: something done unexpectedly comes out in a surprising order
to inhale is to take in, so one piece is drawn inside another

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged
a chamber pot is a pot, so chamber stands for it

explanation.surface: Someone surprisingly decided to smoke cannabis, with reverberating consequences.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pot' and 'inhale' conjure cannabis, but the pot is the bedroom kind kept under the bed.
explanation.definitionFit: Echo chambers are rooms built to produce reverberation, where sounds bounce back repeatedly off the walls.

clue.text: Being caught probing religious ascetic

indicators.note: a probe is pushed inside something, so one piece goes into another

blocks.note: the Essenes were an ascetic Jewish sect
C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: Someone is caught prying into the life of a religious hermit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Being' looks like a verb but it is the noun for one's nature. The Essenes were an ascetic sect in Judea around the time of Christ.
explanation.definitionFit: A thing's essence is its fundamental nature or inner self, which is one philosophical sense of being.

clue.text: Program linked to a reduced kind of plants

indicators.note: reduced means cut down, so the word loses its last letter

blocks.note: a bot is an automated software program
taken as written
nice means kind; its final E goes

explanation.surface: A computer program associated with a pared-down variety of plants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kind of plants' reads as a phrase, but 'kind' is the adjective nice and 'of plants' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Botanic is the adjective for botany, the study of vegetation, as in botanic gardens.

clue.text: Short comic piece brother’s written capturing Queen

indicators.note: to capture is to hold inside, so one piece wraps another

blocks.note: sib is short for sibling, a brother
QU is an abbreviation for queen

explanation.surface: A brother has written a little satirical sketch featuring the Queen.
explanation.walkthrough: The ’s means 'is', so the brother is written around the Queen.
explanation.definitionFit: A squib is a brief satirical or humorous piece of writing, named after the small firework.

clue.text: A Parisienne and American together, mostly sleeping? Extremely disquieting

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the last letter is cut

blocks.note: une is the French feminine for 'a'
A is the abbreviation for American
a siesta is an afternoon sleep; its final A goes

explanation.surface: A French woman and an American sharing a bed find it all deeply unsettling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A Parisienne' asks for 'a' in French, and the feminine form UNE. The siesta stands for a spell of sleeping.
explanation.definitionFit: The superlative of uneasy describes whatever causes the most anxiety, so extremely disquieting matches it.

clue.text: Players in soccer game forming line on another pitch?

blocks.note: first meaning: two teams of eleven take the field
second meaning: the line marked 22 metres from each goal line on a rugby field

explanation.surface: Footballers lining up on a different field before a match.
explanation.walkthrough: The other pitch is a rugby pitch, whose 22-metre line is simply called the twenty-two.
explanation.definitionFit: Two football sides of eleven total that number, and rugby players name the line by its distance from goal.

clue.text: Extravagant dish largely avoided during occasion

indicators.note: largely means for the most part, so the final letter drops off
something happening during an event sits inside it

blocks.note: to duck is to avoid, so avoided is ducked, minus its D
a turn is an occasion, as in 'your turn'

explanation.surface: A lavish dish that most people avoided at a special occasion.
explanation.walkthrough: Occasion in the sense of a go or opportunity, as in 'it's your turn', not a celebration.
explanation.definitionFit: A turducken is a deboned chicken stuffed inside a duck inside a turkey, a famously excessive roast.

clue.text: Keen frost wrecked fasteners

indicators.note: something wrecked is smashed apart, so the letters are scattered and rebuilt

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A sharp frost has damaged the clips holding things together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keen' reads as an adjective for a biting frost, but both words are only letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Reef knots are square knots used to tie two rope ends together, so they serve as fastenings.

clue.text: Finished early race, skipping second part of Cheddar Gorge

indicators.note: to skip something is to leave it out, so a letter is omitted

blocks.note: over means finished
a heat is a preliminary race
the second letter of Cheddar, dropped from the race

explanation.surface: A race finished early because runners avoided the climb through Cheddar Gorge.
explanation.walkthrough: Cheddar Gorge is a limestone canyon in Somerset, England, but 'Gorge' here is the verb. HEAT loses its H.
explanation.definitionFit: To gorge is to stuff yourself with food, which is exactly eating too much.

clue.text: Colourful parts of plant, small and mainly slight

indicators.note: mainly means most but not all, so the final letter is cut

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for small
an affront is a slight or insult; its T goes

explanation.surface: Describing bright bits of a plant that are small and mostly delicate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slight' looks like an adjective for small, but it is the noun meaning insult.
explanation.definitionFit: Saffron is the dried orange-red stigmas of the crocus flower, prized as a spice and dye.

clue.text: US farm subdivision not opening for business

indicators.note: without its opening, a word has lost its first letter

blocks.note: a branch is a subdivision of an organisation
surface padding that pins down the kind of subdivision: a business's local office

explanation.surface: An American farm's new section that isn't yet open for trade.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface splits naturally as 'not opening for business', but 'for business' belongs with subdivision: a business's local branch.
explanation.definitionFit: A ranch is a large North American estate for raising cattle or other livestock.

clue.text: Performing for men in unit

indicators.note: one thing being in another puts it inside

blocks.note: one is a single unit
a stag party is for men only

explanation.surface: A soldier serving in a military unit for the men.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unit' suggests an army unit, but it is the number one. A stag do is a British bachelor party.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone on stage is in front of an audience giving a performance, so the phrase fits.

clue.text: Jelly son consumed in a shot

indicators.note: something consumed is taken inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for son
A plus pic, a photograph or shot

explanation.surface: A boy wolfing down jelly, captured in a photograph.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shot' looks like a drink but it is a photograph, a pic.
explanation.definitionFit: Aspic is a savoury jelly made from meat stock, used to set cold dishes.

clue.text: Look at sites, backing corporation’s slice

indicators.note: backing means moving backwards, so the word is read the other way

blocks.note: to surf the web is to browse websites
a corporation is old slang for a pot belly, a tum

explanation.surface: Checking sites while supporting a company's share of the market.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corporation' is a jokey old word for a paunch, not a company. 'Backing' reads as support but turns SURF round.
explanation.definitionFit: A frustum is the part of a cone or pyramid left between two parallel cutting planes, a geometric section.

clue.text: Figure of speech elevated by English Left

indicators.note: elevated means raised up, so in a down answer the letters climb upwards

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for English
port is the left side of a ship

explanation.surface: An English politician of the Left promoting a fashionable turn of phrase.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' looks political, with its capital letter, but it is the nautical port.
explanation.definitionFit: A trope is a rhetorical device such as metaphor, using words in a non-literal way.

clue.text: Spring not entirely long? There’s an extra day in it

definitions.text: There’s an extra day in it

indicators.note: not entirely means falling short of the whole, so the last letter goes

blocks.note: to spring is to leap
to long is to yearn; its N goes

explanation.surface: Spring feels short, or long, and there is an extra day in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spring' looks like the season and 'long' like a length of time; they are the verbs leap and yearn.
explanation.definitionFit: Every fourth calendar year has 29 February added, giving 366 days instead of the usual 365.

clue.text: Krypton, oxygen, neon and tin from Scandinavia

blocks.note: Kr is the chemical symbol for krypton
O is the chemical symbol for oxygen
Ne is the chemical symbol for neon

explanation.surface: A list of chemical elements: three gases and a metal mined in Scandinavia.
explanation.walkthrough: Tin is the metal Sn alongside the gases, but here it is British slang for money.
explanation.definitionFit: The krone is the currency of Denmark and Norway, and tin is slang for cash.

clue.text: Twice note collapses in funds for Durham town

indicators.note: something that collapses falls into disorder, so the letters are rearranged
one thing being in another places it inside

blocks.note: the word note written two times
stocks are funds or financial holdings

explanation.surface: Twice, a banknote crashes in value within money set aside for a northern town.
explanation.walkthrough: The doubled NOTE is rearranged and then sits inside STOCKS.
explanation.definitionFit: Stockton-on-Tees is an industrial town in north-east England, historically within County Durham.
